title: Resident cache floorplanner — fragmentation mitigation and reclamation playbook (draft)
content:
Context:

This is a working draft describing a small-footprint floorplanner and reclamation playbook for the resident KV cache that prioritizes low tail latency and tenant isolation while minimizing internal fragmentation. It tries to bridge two threads: (1) we want a compact, slab-friendly layout for short-lived slices (kv entries + variable sized values) and (2) we need bounded-cost compaction/reclaim that plays nicely with request-side SLOs.

Goals and constraints (high level):
- Keep per-request median and 99.9 latency within SLOs; reclamation cannot block hot-path allocations for > ~50us on critical GPUs.
- Reduce long-term fragmentation (internal/external) without heavy background GC sweeps that spike GPU memory usage or steal cycles during peak.
- Support multi-tenant fairness (slots, prefixes, tenants) and per-tenant soft quotas with backpressure signals to router.
- Allow incremental rollout (can enable per-shard) and operational observability (metrics + tracepoints).

Terminology (quick):
- slot: smallest alloc unit for stored value payloads (configurable: 256B/1KB/4KB depending on pool).
- span: contiguous run of slots allocated to an object.
- floorplanner: layout decision logic that decides which pool/shape to allocate from and whether to trigger compaction hints.
- breadcrumb metadata: compact, per-span tags used to record access hotness, tenant id, and prefix affinity used by eviction/compaction heuristics.

Design overview:
1) Heterogeneous slot pools (slab-ish but flexible)
   - Pools by granularity: tiny(256B), small(1KB), medium(4KB), large(16KB). Each pool uses a compact free-list with a small bitmap per page to track used slots.
   - New: introduce "morphing pages" — pages which can be reinterpreted at runtime between small/medium sizing via a cheap header mapping (for workloads with shifting size distributions). Morphing avoids prefrag-bias.

2) Span packing + prefix affinity
   - When creating spans we prefer co-locating entries that share prefix/tenant when possible (heuristic: same prefix last-touch within X seconds) to improve KV-cache locality and make tenant reclamation cheaper.
   - Maintain a per-page prefix histogram (low-res: 64-slot counters) to guide admissions. This is cheap and helps avoid scattering a tenant across many pages which increases fragmentation when the tenant's footprint shrinks.

3) Probabilistic admission + adaptation layer (floorplanner decisions)
   - Admission takes into account object size, recent hotness (breadcrumb), and per-tenant soft quota. If a large object would leave tiny residual holes that cause >Y% page waste, the floorplanner will redirect it to the large pool or trigger a compaction hint.
   - Use moving-window estimators for size distribution per-shard; adapt pool bucket counts (grow/shrink number of pages per pool) during low-load windows.

4) Eviction and reclamation primitives
   - Eviction is multi-tiered: (A) lightweight LRU-like selection inside page (age + last-touch), (B) page-level eviction candidates (pages with low hotness score and high free ratio), (C) compaction candidates — pages that are fragmented but contain many live small spans.
   - Compaction model: "stealable-slot compaction" — rather than moving all live items at once, compaction proceeds by moving a bounded number of spans to a destination page and marking source slots as forwarded. Forwarding is handled by a tiny indirection layer in the per-key metadata to avoid long stop-the-world pointer rewrites.
   - Deferred reclamation tokens: compaction work is issued as small tokens that are scheduled on background compaction workers with local CPU/GPU budget. Tokens are prioritized by SLO risk and tenant fairness score.

5) Fragmentation-aware eviction policies
   - Introduce "hole inflation" metric: fraction of page capacity wasted by small dead fragments. Pages with high hole inflation get compaction priority even if their raw free ratio is modest.
   - Policy weights: hotness_decay, tenant_penalty, prefix_cohesion, hole_inflation. We experimentally pick weights per workload with an offline simulator (see sim notes).

6) NUMA / device placement and allocation hints
   - For Dedicated mode where a node has multiple GPUs we maintain per-GPU pools and a lightweight routing table. The floorplanner tries to place spans so that requests routed to GPU-A are likely to find cache hits on GPU-A. On bursts, cross-GPU prefetchs are deprioritized.

Operational controls and observability:
- Metrics to expose: page_free_ratio, hole_inflation, compaction_tokens_queued, compaction_latency_p50/p95, tenant_cohesion_index, spans_forwarded, forwarding_miss_rate, morphing_events.
- Traces: allocation path + floorplanner decision tag, compaction token lifecycle.
- Admin controls: per-shard compaction_budget (tokens/sec), emergency_compact_threshold (hole_inflation), tenant_soft_quota_adjust, morphing_enabled flag.

Sim results (short summary):
- Toyed with workload: 60% tiny, 30% small, 10% large; churn=high (median TTL 12s). Baseline (current slab pools without morphing/compaction) shows 18% wasted memory and compaction spikes.
- With floorplanner + morphing + tokenized compaction: average wasted memory ~6%, background compaction CPU overhead ~3% and no 99.9 latency regressions in simulated arrival bursts.
- Notes: simulator is naive; we need to re-run with real trace replay (Jan QPS traces) before rolling to production.

Implementation sketch (components):
- floorplanner service (in-shard): maps allocation requests -> pool, may return compaction hint. lightweight, lock-free fast path (atomic pick of page).
- page metadata: header including occupancy bitmap (popcount fast-path), prefix_histogram(64 counters), hotness_age(uint32 decayed), morph_state. Kept compact to fit into cache lines.
- forwarding indirection: per-key 16-bit forward token stored in key metadata; token points to destination span index within shard (or 0 for none). Extra check happens on lookup (small branch).
- compaction worker: async worker pool (configurable threads per shard) that pulls tokens and moves spans using GC-friendly copy and atomic forward publish. Uses write barrier to ensure readers either see old or new location.

Safety, correctness and SLO considerations:
- Readers must tolerate forwarded entries: lookup semantics check forward token and follow at most 1-2 hops (prevent chained forwards by preferring direct atomic publish).
- Rolling restarts: morph_state persisted in shard checkpoint; if step-down occurs during compaction token on GPU, the token is retried on other worker.
- Metrics backpressure: when compaction backlog exceeds threshold, router is signaled to slow down new admissions or route to fallback model variant.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- How to choose default slot sizes? Suggest small (1KB) as dominant default but need auto-tuning. Need offline runs with Jan/Feb traces.
- Cost accounting: how do we bill/meter compaction CPU/GPU time for Dedicated customers? Should be included under infra or offered as opt-in?
- Forwarding indirection size: 16-bit might overflow for shards with >65k spans; maybe use 32-bit but keep aligned optimizations. Tradeoff: metadata blowup vs safety.
- Morphing correctness under concurrent alloc/free — need formal invariant sketch and unit tests.

Action items (next short sprint):
- [Ava] run trace replay with morphing toggled and capture hole_inflation per-shard (2d).
- [Miguel] prototype forwarding indirection and microbench the lookup overhead (1d).
- [Priya] update observability dashboard template and add compaction token tracing (3d).
- [All] plan canary rollout: shard-by-shard with compaction budget conservative (5 tokens/sec) for first 2 weeks.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on formal proofs; focus on operational safety and low-latency behaviour. Expect design iteration after we get real trace runs.
- Please comment in-line or drop major suggestions in the linked slack thread.

End of draft.
